body:
The Federal Reserve held its target federal funds interest rate in the 3.50%-3.75% range at its July meeting, a decision investors generally expected. Nine members voted to leave the rate unchanged, while three members dissented, favoring a 0.25% hike. Ahead of the decision, investors expected a 35% chance of a rate increase. Elevated inflation, primarily stemming from higher energy prices, increased investor expectations for higher policy rates later this year. Investors now anticipate between [...] anticipate between one and two rate hikes by the end of 2026. [...] Key takeaways

   The U.S. Federal Reserve (Fed) kept its policy interest rate at a range of 3.50%-3.75% citing somewhat tighter financial conditions through higher market-based rates.

   Kevin Warsh made no change to the previous, shortened Fed statement in his second meeting as Fed Chair, and reiterated the Fed’s 2% inflation target and the importance of restoring Fed credibility after years above that target.

The Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.50% to 3.75% this Wednesday, July 29th, 2026, where it has remained since December, in a 9-3 vote. A hold was the market’s base case, but it was not fully priced, as rate futures assigned roughly a one-in-three probability to a hike before the meeting, with those odds moving alongside oil prices through July. The committee was weighing persistent inflation risks against softer recent data. Oil had risen sharply, and policymakers had identified [...] In the immediate reaction to the decision, short-term rate futures and Treasury yields moved lower as markets unwound some of the probability of a near-term hike. As Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference unfolded, however, the 10- and 30-year yields reversed higher even as shorter maturities remained lower, creating tension between a less hawkish expected policy path and renewed concern at the long end. For commercial real estate (CRE) borrowers, that combination offset some of the hawkish [...] depend on whether liquidity, lender competition, and credit demand remain strong enough to offset any renewed pressure from benchmark rates.

## The Federal Reserve left the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.50%–3.75% for a fifth consecutive meeting in July 2026, in line with expectations, despite markets assigning roughly a one-in-three probability to a rate hike. Notably, three FOMC members dissented, preferring to raise the policy rate by 25 basis points, which leaves the door open to a rate increase in September.
